extra.message: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection

metadata.proof: SOURCE: `request.body` is attacker-controlled XML. SINK: Line 196 configures `XMLParser(load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False)`, and line 197 parses the body with it. metadata.proof: SOURCE: Line 145 takes `name` from `request.GET`. SINK: Lines 146-148 join it with `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` and write `request.body` to the resulting path. An attacker sending `?name=../../app/shell.py` writes arbitrary content to any writable location, enabling code execution.

extra.message: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

extra.message: NoSQL Injection via Unvalidated MongoDB Query

extra.message: Permissive CORS with Credentials (Origin Reflection)

extra.message: Missing Authentication on Payroll Operation Endpoint

extra.message: Explicitly Disabled Browser XSS Filter and Content Security Policy

metadata.proof: payroll_frame_slip_423 deliberately sets X-XSS-Protection: 0 (disabling the browser's reflected-XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy: "" (removing any CSP that would otherwise restrict script execution, framing, or data exfiltration). This actively weakens browser security controls for the response, enabling XSS, clickjacking, and data-theft attacks. Requires the ops token but cripples downstream response safety.

extra.message: Improper Certificate Validation — SSL Verification Disabled

metadata.proof: payroll_trust_drift_433 creates an SSL context with _create_unverified_context(), which disables TLS certificate hostname and chain validation for the subsequent urllib.request.urlopen() call to 'https://partner.invalid/status'. This opens the outbound HTTPS connection to man-in-the-middle attacks: any proxy between the server and the remote host can present a self-signed certificate and intercept/modify the response.

extra.message: CSV Formula Injection via Employee Name in Payroll Export

metadata.proof: Employee first_name/last_name from CSV import (lines 148-149, 159-160) are stored directly without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula prefixes (=, +, -, @). When payroll CSV is exported, emp.user.display_name (constructed from first_name + last_name) is written to CSV verbatim at line 264. If a name starts with =CMD|..., =HYPERLINK(...), or =WEBSERVICE(...), opening the CSV in Excel/LibreOffice executes those formulas, leading to RCE or data exfiltration.

extra.message: Hardcoded Authentication Verifier Credentials in Source Code

metadata.proof: The credential verifiers '4812' and '5930' are hardcoded as plaintext string literals at line 118. These values are used to authenticate handle/verifier pairs at line 121 (if verifier != known[handle]). An attacker who obtains source code access — via source-code leak, insider threat, or a previous path-traversal — can read these hardcoded secrets and bypass the verifier-based authentication. Even without source access, the trivial entropy (4-digit numbers) makes brute-force feasible after enumerating the two handles ('north', 'south').

extra.message: Hardcoded Demo Password Used to Create All Seed User Accounts

metadata.proof: The constant DEMO_PASSWORD = 'password-1234' is hardcoded at line 45 and passed as the password argument to User.objects.create_user() for the bootstrap superuser (line 214) and all demo accounts (hr.admin, payroll.lead, manager.demo, employee.demo, plus 22 seeded employees). If this management command is ever run in a non-development environment — or if an attacker with access to the source repo clones the project — every demo account uses the well-known password 'password-1234', allowing complete account takeover across all roles including superuser.

extra.message: Hardcoded Development Secret Key Fallback Exposes Application to Session Forgery

metadata.proof: The settings module hard-codes a development SECRET_KEY when DJANGO_DEBUG is truthy and the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY env var is missing. This key is used by Django's crypto signing (sessions, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens, invite token HMAC seeds). An attacker who knows this static string can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens, and invite-token HMACs, leading to full account compromise. The fallback activates on every deployment where DJANGO_DEBUG=1 and DJANGO_SECRET_KEY is not explicitly set.

extra.message: Hardcoded Default PostgreSQL Password in Settings

metadata.proof: The DATABASES['default']['PASSWORD'] value falls back to the hardcoded string 'hr_portal' when the POSTGRES_PASSWORD env var is absent. This credential is used to authenticate against the PostgreSQL database. An attacker who can reach the database port (default localhost:5432) and knows the default password can read/write all HR data including employee PII, salary records, and user password hashes.

extra.message: Unconditional Console Email Backend Leaks Password Reset Tokens and Invite Links to Stdout

metadata.proof: The EMAIL_BACKEND setting is unconditionally set to the console backend (not conditional on DEBUG). Every email the application sends — including password-reset links (containing raw tokens via PortalPasswordResetView) and employee invitation links (containing raw invite tokens via invite_create) — is written to stdout as plaintext. Any process/operator with access to the application's stdout or log capture infrastructure can extract these tokens and reset any user's password or accept any employee invitation without authorization.

extra.message: CSV Formula Injection in Policy Acknowledgements Export

metadata.proof: emp.user.display_name is constructed from user.first_name + ' ' + user.last_name, which can contain formula-starting characters (e.g., '=cmd|'/C calc'!A0') injected via the CSV employee import where first_name/last_name are taken from CSV rows without formula sanitization. a.policy.code and a.policy.title are also user-controlled via PolicyForm which applies no formula-character sanitization. csv.writer(_Echo()) produces raw CSV output with no prefixing of formula-starting characters ('=', '+', '-', '@'). When the exported CSV is opened in Excel/LibreOffice/Google Sheets, cells starting with =/+/-/@ will be interpreted as spreadsheet formulas and executed client-side.

extra.message: Missing Rate Limiting on Login and Password Reset Endpoints Enables Brute-Force Attacks

metadata.proof: SOURCE: PortalLoginView (line 55), PortalPasswordResetView (line 101), PortalPasswordResetConfirmView (line 119), change_password_view (line 153), and invite_accept (line 232) all inherit from or use Django class-based or function-based auth views with NO throttling, account lockout, or CAPTCHA. SINK: An attacker can submit unlimited POST requests to /accounts/login/ with guessed credentials; each failure is audited but not blocked. Combined with hardcoded demo passwords (seed_data.py creates all accounts with 'password-1234'), this makes credential stuffing and brute-force attacks trivial. No DRF throttling, django-ratelimit, or custom middleware is configured.

extra.message: Cookie Set Without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite Flags Enables Session Sniffing and XSS Token Theft

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The payroll_crumb_lane_290 view sets a cookie named 'portal_crumb' using Django's default set_cookie() which omits HttpOnly (JavaScript accessible via document.cookie), Secure (sent over HTTP when DEBUG), and SameSite (no same-origin restriction) flags. The marker value comes directly from the GET parameter 'marker' (user-controlled). SINK: An attacker who can inject XSS into any page on the same domain can read this cookie. On non-HTTPS connections (DEBUG mode), the cookie is transmitted in clear text. An attacker can also poison the cookie with arbitrary content via the user-controlled marker parameter.

extra.message: CSRF Protection Disabled on POST API Endpoint That Accepts Session Authentication

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The @csrf_exempt decorator at line 201 disables Django's CSRF middleware for this POST handler. SINK: The _auth_user_for_json() helper (line 29) first checks request.user.is_authenticated (session-based cookie auth). A victim authenticated via session cookies who visits a malicious page can have that page submit a cross-origin POST to /api/v1/dev/echo/ and the request will be processed under the victim's identity because CSRF middleware is bypassed. The echoed payload could be used for data exfiltration via response timing or reflected content.

extra.message: Existing Sessions Not Invalidated When User is Disabled or Role-Changed

metadata.proof: SOURCE: admin_user_toggle_active (line 393-394) toggles is_active, and admin_user_edit (line 359) saves user/role changes. SINK: Both save() calls complete without invalidating the target user's existing sessions (no Session.objects.filter(user=target).delete() or equivalent). Django's AuthenticationMiddleware does not check is_active on each request, and bare @login_required decorators (profile_view at line 150, change_password_view at line 163) do not block disabled users. A disabled user with a valid session cookie can still access their profile and change their password for the full SESSION_COOKIE_AGE (8 hours).
